title: The Wise Men of Chelm, the Stove and the Letter
summary: Little Gitele strolls through Chelm with a note in her mitten and meets two great pieces of Chelm wisdom: a giant sign on the study-house stove so thieves won't take it, and a scribe writing a letter in enormous letters so his faraway uncle can read it. And what did Gitele write to Grandma? Two short jokes in one rhyming story, based on traditional tales of the Wise Men of Chelm.
pages:
Gitele went for a walk in Chelm, a note in her red mitten, small,
she looked at everything, being clever, and asked about it all.
And there in the study house stood a stove, black and warm,
with fancy painted letters on it, a name in festive form.

Yokel the shammes polished the stove and read out, loud and grand:
"THE STOVE BELONGS TO THE STUDY HOUSE!" in letters sky-high to stand.
"But why write that?" asked Gitele, as serious as could be.
And Yokel peeked to the right and left, and whispered secretly:

"We're afraid of thieves!" said Yokel, and his eyes grew round and wide.
"A thief will read the sign and go home — no stove, but satisfied."

The stove is heavy as a mountain, and fat, and round, and hot,
and ten thieves couldn't budge it — but the sign is there, like it or not.
That's how it is in Chelm: for every thing, a reason why,
and Gitele laughed and went to look for the next, by and by.

Out in the street, by the corner well, Reb Lipa the scribe sat writing,
each letter like a plate, each letter like a story — how exciting!
His quill was like a broom, his ink a bucket full and deep,
his paper spread across the whole street — what a wonder, what a heap!

"Why are the letters so big?" asked Gitele, with eyes as round as can be.
"I'm writing to my uncle," said Reb Lipa, "who lives far, far from me,
past the river, and the mountain, and the forest, and more, you see."

"If I write small, he won't see! The distance, as everyone knows, is great.
But he'll read every word from far away if each letter's as big as a plate."
That's how it is in Chelm: for every thing, a reason why,
and Gitele laughed and went to look for the next, by and by.

The letters grew and grew, like dough that rises high:
one like a wagon wheel, one like a door, one bigger still — oh my!
The paper crawled up to the rooftops, Reb Lipa climbed a ladder tall,
and the children laughed below and held it steady so he wouldn't fall.

On a faraway mountain, almost at the edge of the world,
the uncle stood with a spyglass and read every letter as the paper unfurled.
That's how it is in Chelm: for every thing, a reason why,
and Gitele laughed and went to look for the next, by and by.

Gitele remembered the note in her red mitten and opened it with care,
and it was tiny-tiny, like a mouse, with teeny letters there.
The note was for Grandma, who lived in the house close by,
just two steps from here — and Gitele held it up high.

Reb Lipa and Yokel peeked over her shoulder, and their mouths fell open wide:
"Such tiny letters? Who could read them? Who? What?" they cried.
And Grandma, at her window, put on her glasses and read it all, calm and slow,
and blew Gitele a kiss, as sweet as Shabbat-morning cake, you know.

And the stove guards itself, with dignity, beneath its long sign,
and the letter's spread over the rooftops, still on its way to the uncle, line by line.
That's how it is in Chelm: for every thing, a reason why —
and Gitele wrote small, because her Grandma lives close by.
